Thresholds, tolerances and measurement windows are modelled generically because the cloud SLA standard normally relied on (ISO/IEC 19086-1) returned HTTP 403 and could not be read. Only UNIDROIT 5.1.6 reasonable-quality grounding is primary; treat the SLO shape as unsupported structure pending retrieval.

Register upkeep, currency and accessibility requirements rest on the ISO 37301 committee scope statement only; the normative clause text is paywalled and was not read, so review cadence, escalation and register completeness requirements are presented as practice, not as cited normative requirements.
Place of performance with stated-versus-default indicator, jurisdictional territory and subject-matter extent, and ODRL spatial operands. Grounded in UNIDROIT 6.1.6 and LegalRuleML Jurisdiction.

Place of performance is a reference into a location or party model rather than a geometry; no coordinate reference system, precision or topology requirement arises from the sources for a general obligation mixin.

Integrity digests chained across append-only logs, quarantine of artefacts failing integrity checks, verification of external proofs without re-signing, and authority requirements for state assertions.
Personal data flag, lawful basis, minimised evaluator access, and separately reportable access to personal data. Grounded in GDPR Articles 6(1)(c) and 30.

Assignment of rights, transfer of duties, delegation of performance and novation, each with consent or notice requirements, release status and an explicit identity continuity rule. Grounded in UNIDROIT Chapter 9.

known_omissions: ISO/IEC 19086-1 (cloud SLA framework, service level objectives and service qualitative objectives) could not be retrieved; the standard's page returned HTTP 403. The performance-standard finding therefore lacks the primary grounding that would normally define threshold, metric and measurement-window structure.
The normative text of ISO 37301:2021 is paywalled; only the ISO/TC 309 committee scope statement was read. Obligations-register requirements are therefore treated as gap-level support.

Multiagent commitment-protocol literature that formalises the operations create, cancel, release, delegate and assign over C(debtor, creditor, antecedent, consequent) could not be machine-read (the AAMAS commitment-alignment PDF failed to parse). The state model is grounded in ODRL, LegalRuleML and UNIDROIT, with the achievement-versus-maintenance distinction taken from the AAAI 2021 abstract only; the finer-grained commitment operations are deliberately not asserted.

The OMG SBVR specification page yielded title, version and date but not the clause text on deontic and alethic modality; the distinction as used here is supported at the level of SBVR's stated purpose plus secondary commentary, so the violability filter is a weaker claim than the ODRL and LegalRuleML groundings.
Insolvency effects on obligations — automatic stay, set-off on insolvency, subordination and rescission of preferences — are not modelled and would materially change enforceability.
Tax, prudential and sector-specific statutory obligation catalogues are not enumerated; only GDPR is used as a worked statutory example.

Non-Western and non-commercial obligation frameworks (Shariah-compliant structures, customary and community obligations, family-law duties) are not addressed; the model's grounding is commercial and regulatory.

Distributed-ledger or self-executing settlement semantics are treated as an interface projection and are not modelled; automated execution introduces determinism and finality questions this model does not answer.
Negotiation and pre-contractual commitments (letters of intent, memoranda of understanding, comfort letters) are not distinguished from binding commitments beyond the violability filter.
Aggregate and portfolio-level views — exposure across obligations, netting, and covenant baskets — are out of scope; this model describes one obligation at a time.
FIBO FND Law LegalCapacity contingent-obligation and condition-precedent properties were only snippet-searched, not fetched as a full ontology, so clause-linkage details are a gap.
Assignment, delegation and novation of obligations are not specified in the fetched UNIDROIT chapter 7 section 1; likely belong to a sibling transfer/novation model.
Joint and several liability multiplicity is asked but not grounded in a primary multiplicity scheme beyond FIBO party-role cardinality.
Prescription, limitation periods and death/incapacity of the obligor lack primary support in the fetched set.
CISG Article 33 (time of performance) is the acknowledged inspiration for UNIDROIT 6.1.1 but was not fetched.
ISO 37301 compliance-management obligations and ISO 22600-2 (cited by HL7) were not fetched as primary texts.
Smart-contract oracle fulfilment, Islamic finance consideration rules, and criminal-law duties are out of the fetched corpus.
DPROD dutyState is an emerging profile, not W3C ODRL core; using it as canonical state without a Dimension declaration would be over-claim.
Hohfeld correlatives are treated only via LegalRuleML Right and FIBO reciprocity, not via a jurisprudence primary text.
conflicts: ODRL requires exactly one target Asset on a Permission and a Prohibition, and models actions as operations on assets. Many legal and regulatory obligations (file a return, maintain insurance, appoint an officer) have no asset. ODRL's Duty allows zero-or-one target, so duties remain expressible, but any projection that routes obligations through permissions will misfit; recorded as a divergence rather than resolved.

ODRL forbids a consequence Duty from itself carrying a consequence, and forbids a remedy from referring to a Duty that includes a consequence. Legal escalation chains are open-ended (interest on unpaid damages, penalties on unpaid penalties). This model recurses onto itself for secondary obligations and therefore cannot round-trip deep escalation chains through ODRL without flattening; the flattening strategy must be recorded.

LegalRuleML models a Right as a Permission to a bearer implying obligations on auxiliary parties, while FIBO models a Commitment as a promise giving rise to both an obligation and a reciprocal right. The modelling unit differs — a normative statement versus a promise — so a one-to-one mapping between LegalRuleML Right and FIBO Commitment must not be assumed.

The IFRS 15 sense of performance obligation is narrower than the legal sense: it covers only promises to transfer distinct goods or services to a customer, and obligations falling outside it are addressed by other standards. Treating the accounting flag as a general obligation classifier would misclassify most regulatory and internal obligations.

ODRL distinguishes a policy-level obligation from a duty attached as a pre-condition of a permission, with different fulfilment consequences. Collapsing both into a single obligation field loses the distinction between a freestanding duty and a duty that gates an entitlement.

RFC 3339 requires an explicit offset, but many legal deadlines are stated in local civil time with a business-day convention and no offset. Canonicalising to a UTC instant at capture destroys legally relevant information; this model retains both representations, which means the canonical instant alone is not authoritative for deadline disputes.

ODRL requires a processing system to stop when it does not recognise a profile identifier, whereas obligation registers commonly need best-effort ingestion of partially understood external policies. Silent partial processing would breach the ODRL requirement; the model therefore requires an explicit halt-and-quarantine rather than lenient parsing.
ODRL fulfilment is binary exercise of an action; UNIDROIT non-performance includes defective and late performance of an otherwise exercised action. Do not collapse these tests.
IAS 37 recognises constructive obligations; US GAAP Topic 450 generally does not under the same model. Overlay fields must not be overwritten across bases.
XACML/HL7/FHIR 'obligation' is a mandated operation or conformance behaviour beside an access or data-handling decision, not a contractual Duty.
ODRL consequence keeps the original duty required; some commercial practices treat liquidated damages as substituting for performance. Record the rule actually adopted.
LegalRuleML Prohibition as [OBL]-p versus ODRL Prohibition as a disjoint Rule subclass: forbearance modelling will not round-trip without an explicit map.
IFRS 15 performance-obligation satisfaction (control transfer) is not the same as ODRL Duty fulfilment or UNIDROIT due performance.
regional_assumptions: The UNIDROIT Principles are soft law: they apply where the parties choose them, where they supplement an international instrument, or as gap-fillers. Their rules on best efforts, conditions, place and currency of performance, force majeure, hardship, assignment, limitation and plurality are used here as a well-attested reference frame, not as universally binding law.

Limitation periods, survival rules and the enforceability of penalty and liquidated-damages clauses vary materially by jurisdiction; several common-law systems restrict penalty clauses that civil-law systems permit. Specific durations and enforceability outcomes must be determined per governing law and are deliberately not asserted here.

GDPR-derived retention, erasure and lawful-basis structure applies to personal data within EU and EEA scope. Other regimes impose different retention floors and erasure rights, so the retention finding's mechanics are portable but its specific bases are not.

IFRS 15 applies where IFRS Accounting Standards are used; converged but non-identical national standards exist elsewhere, and jurisdictions on local GAAP may define performance obligations differently or not at all.

Business-day conventions, public holidays and civil-time offsets are jurisdiction-specific and are referenced from a calendar model rather than defined here; deadline computation is only as correct as that reference.

Notice service rules, including what counts as effective service and when it takes effect, are jurisdiction-specific; the model records service evidence and instants but does not assert validity of service.
UNIDROIT Principles are an international commercial-law restatement, not domestic mandatory law; local civil-code or common-law rules may add consideration, privity or formality requirements.
IAS 37/IFRS 15 overlays assume IFRS reporting; US GAAP and other GAAPs differ on constructive obligations and contingency thresholds.
LegalRuleML encodings are jurisdiction-neutral carriers of jurisdiction-specific norms; jurisdiction-code is an annotation, not a world-law identifier.
ODRL is a web policy language widely used for rights, not a substitute for private-law obligation in courts.
HL7/FHIR obligation codes reflect health-interoperability practice and must not be generalised as legal duties.
adversarial_checks: Counterexample — commitment with no identified beneficiary. FIBO recognises a commitment at large made without direct involvement of potential beneficiaries. The model therefore makes the obligee reference optional (0..n) and adds an explicit directedness code, rather than requiring a counterparty as most contract-centric designs do.

Counterexample — negative obligation. A duty to refrain is violated by performing the act, not by omitting it. A single boolean 'fulfilled' flag would be meaningless here, so violation polarity is a required element and forbearance is flagged on the action, keeping prohibition semantics from being silently coerced into obligation semantics.

Counterexample — obligation with no asset. Statutory duties such as appointing a data protection officer or responding within one month have no target asset. Target references are therefore 0..n with an explicit assertion available for the target-free case, and the ODRL asset-targeting divergence is recorded rather than papered over.

Counterexample — maintenance obligation. A duty to keep insurance in force is not discharged by a single act and cannot be modelled by a due date plus a completion flag. The achievement/maintenance axis is a required classification and the state model requires transient lapse to be distinguishable from terminal breach.

Counterexample — obligation that is owed but unenforceable. Limitation and survival are modelled separately from discharge, so an obligation can be substantively outstanding while time-barred, which a simple open/closed state model cannot express.

Rejected structure — a priority, urgency or workload layer. Attractive for operations, but these are attributes of the work item that discharges the obligation, not of the duty itself; admitting them would duplicate the task model and make obligation records vary with staffing.

Rejected structure — a smart-contract or automation-execution layer. Self-execution is a property of a projection and an interface, not of the obligation's semantics; including it would violate the format-neutrality requirement and embed finality assumptions the sources do not support.

Rejected structure — an accounting recognition and provisioning layer. IFRS 15's boundary makes clear that recognition and measurement are a separate discipline; the model carries only the performance-obligation flag and the distinctness assessment, and refers the rest out.

Conflation test — obligation versus requirement or control. A compliance requirement in a register and an instantiated duty on a named bearer are different objects with different lifecycles; the model describes one entry and explicitly excludes control design and assurance results, keeping the register aggregation in a sibling model.

Overreach test — conformance claims. Every alignment is stated as a mapping with a relation and recorded conflicts, and the service layer forbids asserting conformance without a dated validation report, so no node in this structure claims standard conformance on the strength of resemblance alone.

Support test — every layer traced to primary sources. Two dimensions failed this test and are marked as gaps rather than presented as canonical: service-level objective structure (ISO/IEC 19086-1 unreachable) and obligations-register operations (ISO 37301 clause text paywalled).
If an English label 'obligation' is used as a join key across ODRL, XACML and IAS 37, legally distinct senses will be merged; deontic-kind-code is the falsifier.
If fulfilment is stored as a boolean without performance-quality-code, defective and late performance required by UNIDROIT 7.1.1 become invisible.
If due dates are used as identifiers or stored as timezone-naive dates, overdue evaluation is not reproducible across regions.
If consequence duties replace the original duty by default, the instance is not ODRL-compatible even if labelled as such.
If FHIR SHALL-handle-field codes are treated as contractual commitments, healthcare conformance will be misread as legal liability.
If IAS 37 recognition is taken as proof that no obligation exists when outflow is not probable, deontic duties will disappear from operations while still binding at law.

boundaryDecision.rationale: Both providers independently arrived at mixin, and the base scope statement, ten boundary notes and explicit out-of-scope list draw complete lines against the agreement instrument, party master data, the policy/rule container, task execution, payment and settlement mechanics, dispute management, control registers and accounting recognition. The base also passes the definitional/alethic filter (SBVR) that keeps non-violable necessities out of the register. The only boundary pressure in this adjudication is the imported access-control and conformance obligation sense, which is admitted as a crosswalk alignment entry only, leaving the base exclusion of decision-point and evaluation infrastructure intact.

decisions.rationale: The base carries ten boundary notes, an explicit out-of-scope list and adversarial counterexamples (commitment at large, negative duty, asset-free statutory duty, maintenance duty, owed-but-time-barred duty) that close the model edges. The alternative's seven notes are sound but leave party roles, stewardship, provenance and retention thin. Node count was not decisive; edge completeness was.

Both providers independently classified the entry as a mixin attachable to contracts, statutes, licences, orders, policies and unilateral commitments, and neither structure carries instrument formation, party identity or ledger semantics that would force a standalone entity.

Tier-1 primary grounding for two obligation homonyms absent from the base crosswalk; admitted as mapping and sense-disambiguation only, with the source finding's access and retention material dropped as duplicative of base access-and-retention.

decisions.concept: IAS 37 provision recognition and measurement overlay
decisions.rationale: The base explicitly out-of-scopes accounting recognition and measurement and draws a boundary note to Liability/Provision. Importing provision amount, risk adjustment, discounting and onerous-contract testing would reopen a deliberately closed edge and duplicate a sibling financial-reporting model.

decisions.concept: IAS 37 legal versus constructive obligation classification
decisions.rationale: Adjacent to but not identical with the base external-versus-voluntary origin axis from ISO 37301. Deciding whether constructive obligation is an origin class of the duty or only a recognition trigger requires primary clause text neither provider read, so it is not bolted onto obligation-typology on inference.

Tier-3 non-primary profile, and the source provider itself flags adopting it as canonical as an over-claim. The base lifecycle-state-machine is grounded in the ODRL fulfilment test, LegalRuleML Violation/Compliance indications and the achievement/maintenance distinction, which is stronger support.

Place and currency of performance already sit in base subject-and-place, and ordering with reciprocal dependency in finding-composition-and-dependency; importing the finding would fragment place of performance across two nodes. Its one unique element, withholding performance, is deferred to research instead.

Base antecedent-and-detachment plus constraint-expression already carry suspensive and resolutive conditions, detachment evidence and timestamping, improper interference, and the full ODRL Constraint and LogicalConstraint expression form including andSequence ordering.

Base excuse-remedy-consequence already carries the ODRL consequence and remedy nesting prohibitions, LegalRuleML PenaltyStatement and Reparation, cure periods, penalty caps, and the recursion of secondary duties back onto this model as obligations in their own right.

The base already asserts ODRL Validator and Evaluator grounding in its validation checklist dimension and covers competent issuer and evidence sufficiency in fulfilment-evidence; importing the combined evidence finding would create a second evidence node for one extra distinction.

The base recognises cure as a question but exposes no operation between declaring non-performance and applying remedy, so the suspension of inconsistent remedies during an additional period is currently unreachable; grounded in a tier-1 primary source.

Enforcing ObligationExpressions on a Permit or Deny decision is decision-point infrastructure, which the base out-of-scopes. The XACML sense enters as a crosswalk entry only, never as an operation of this mixin.

Follows the same boundary as the rejected IAS 37 overlay: applying provision versus contingent-liability tests is a financial-reporting operation on some obligations, not an operation of the deontic record itself.

Base transition-state applies permitted transitions with authority, basis, event time and observation time, and fulfilment-and-acceptance already enumerates discharge modes including substitute performance, set-off, waiver, release and expiry.

decisions.disposition: recorded as declared divergence, not resolved
decisions.rationale: Both providers independently find that LegalRuleML obligation-of-a-negated-act and the ODRL disjoint Prohibition subclass will not round-trip. The base already records violation polarity and a divergence list, so synthesis keeps this as a crosswalk conflict rather than choosing a winner without primary authority to do so.

The two providers scatter access, retention, validation and interoperability service concerns across different bundles; merging them onto the base's single service surface prevents two competing access-control and retention narratives coexisting in one published model.

publicationHolds: Live-URL and version-pin verification for all fourteen base sources plus the two imported ones (XACML 3.0, HL7 FHIR obligation codes) before any citation is published.

FIBO source conflict: the base pins spec.edmcouncil.org Agreements and Contracts at 'master/latest retrieved 2026-08-23' while the other provider pins raw.githubusercontent.com at versionIRI 20260601. Resolve to one dated release IRI before publication.

UNIDROIT edition pin: the base cites the 2016 black-letter PDF, while the imported cure and additional-period function derives from a 2010 Chapter 7 Section 1 page. Confirm 2016 numbering for Articles 7.1.1 to 7.1.5 before citing them.

Multi-profile domain validation: exercise the mixin against a contract clause, a statutory or regulatory duty, a court or administrative order, an internal voluntary commitment and an access-control or conformance obligation before claiming the alignment holds.

Performance-standard finding remains partially supported: ISO/IEC 19086-1 returned HTTP 403, so thresholds, metrics and measurement windows must be published as generic structure explicitly labelled as lacking primary grounding.

ISO 37301 normative clause text is paywalled and only the committee scope statement was read; register upkeep, review cadence and escalation must be published as practice, not as cited normative requirements.

Confirm the imported XACML and FHIR sense alignment is published as a crosswalk entry only and does not reopen the base exclusion of access-control decision points and their evaluation infrastructure.
No conformance claim to ODRL, LegalRuleML, FIBO, IFRS 15, XACML or FHIR may be published without a dated validation report; alignment relations only until then.
deferredResearch: UNIDROIT 7.1.2: non-performance caused by the other party's act or by a risk it bears, and whether the base needs an explicit interference and risk-allocation defence distinct from the existing condition-interference question.

UNIDROIT 7.1.3 withholding of performance in reciprocal obligations (simultaneous versus consecutive tender) as a distinct pre-remedy state of an unperformed duty, currently absent from both the composition and the non-performance layers.

UNIDROIT 7.2.1 and 7.2.2 limits on specific performance (impossibility, unreasonable burden, reasonable cover from another source, exclusively personal character) and whether they belong to this mixin or to a remedies sibling model.
Whether the IAS 37 constructive obligation and the ISO 37301 voluntary commitment are the same origin axis; requires the normative clause text of both, neither of which was read by either provider.

Multiagent commitment operations (create, cancel, release, delegate, assign) over C(debtor, creditor, antecedent, consequent): the AAMAS commitment-alignment PDF failed to parse, so the finer-grained operations remain unasserted in the state model.

Insolvency effects on enforceability — automatic stay, set-off on insolvency, subordination and rescission of preferences — listed as a base known omission and material to the limitation and survival findings.
DPROD Duty profile status and whether any Dimension declares it, before its Pending/Active/Fulfilled/Violated vocabulary could ever be referenced as more than a third-party profile.

model.name: Time / Calendar
model.purpose: Provide a format-neutral, authority-grounded reference model for temporal reference data (time scales, civil time zones, calendar systems, recurrence, holidays and observances) together with the embeddable temporal value shapes that every other model needs to express instants, intervals, durations, schedules and deadlines unambiguously.
model.scope_statement: WM-XCT-009 is a mix-in plus reference model. It defines (a) the governed reference data that determines what a civil date-time means — time scales and leap adjustments, time zone identifiers and their offset-transition history, calendar systems, eras and week rules, and jurisdictional holidays and observances; and (b) the reusable temporal value shapes (instant, interval, duration, recurrence, precision, binding mode) that sibling models embed. It is storage- and interface-neutral: TZif, iCalendar, JSCalendar, JSON, XML, Git or MongoDB are projections of the same semantics. It records external standards as alignments, never as claimed conformance, and treats the IANA tz database and CLDR as mirrors of civil decisions rather than as the legal authority for them.
in_scope: Time scales, epochs and their mutual offsets (UTC, TAI, UT1, GPS time, POSIX/Unix time), and the governance of leap adjustments
Civil time zone identity, canonical/alias relationships, standard and daylight offsets, and the complete transition history of a zone
Legal instruments and decision processes by which a jurisdiction sets or changes standard time and daylight saving arrangements
Calendar systems and their identifiers, eras and year numbering, intercalation and leap-month structure, and territory week rules
Reusable temporal value shapes: instant, interval, duration, period, granularity/precision, and the floating/zoned/absolute binding contract
Recurrence rule semantics, exceptions and overrides, and calendar-scale-aware recurrence expansion
Public holidays as proclaimed by an authority, cultural and religious observances and their computation methods
Working-day and business-day calendars, weekend rules and date-adjustment (business day) conventions
Reference-data lifecycle: release versioning, signing, distribution, expiry, freshness and correction of temporal reference data
out_of_scope: Clock synchronisation and time transfer protocols and their engineering (NTP, PTP, GNSS timing, UTC(k) traceability chains) — a distinct time-dissemination model
Calendaring and scheduling application semantics such as attendees, invitations, free/busy, alarms and iTIP scheduling workflows
The definition and geometry of jurisdictions and territories themselves — held by the place/jurisdiction model and only referenced here
General identifier-scheme governance — held by the identifier and naming model; this model only consumes registered temporal identifier schemes
Astronomical ephemeris computation and the physics of Earth rotation; only the published results (leap-second decisions, DUT1 limits) are consumed
Labour-law entitlements, pay premiums and leave accrual arising from holidays; only the day-off status of a holiday is modelled
Domain deadline policy (SLA targets, statutory limitation periods); this model supplies the calculus, not the policy
Localisation and formatting of dates for presentation, beyond the identifiers and week/calendar preference data needed to compute correct values

boundary_notes.distinction: Time zones and holidays are scoped to jurisdictions and sub-jurisdictional divisions (for example the UK bank-holiday divisions england-and-wales, scotland, northern-ireland, or US county-level zone boundaries in 49 CFR Part 71). This model references those jurisdiction identities; it does not define territories, boundaries or their geometry. tz zone names are deliberately not country-based and must not be treated as jurisdiction identifiers.

tzids, CLDR BCP47 timezone keys and u-ca calendar keys are governed identifier schemes maintained elsewhere. This model records which scheme an identifier belongs to, its canonical form and its alias relations; scheme registration policy itself belongs to the identifier model.

boundary_notes.neighbor: Time dissemination and clock synchronisation model
boundary_notes.distinction: BIPM Circular T and IERS bulletins are consumed here as authoritative statements about the scale (leap seconds, UTC-TAI, UTC(k) deviations). How a device acquires and steers to that scale, and traceability of a local clock, is a separate engineering model.

RFC 5545 and RFC 8984 are alignments for recurrence and time-zone value semantics only. Event participation, scheduling negotiation and calendar-store synchronisation belong to an application model that embeds this mix-in.

Business day conventions and business-centre holiday calendars are defined here as reusable date arithmetic. Which convention a given contract or instrument elects is a fact of that instrument, held by the financial model.

Reference periods, retention triggers and reporting cut-offs embed this model's interval and recurrence shapes. The meaning of a reference period for a statistic, or of a retention trigger for a record, stays with those models.

sources.title: Time Zone Database (tz database), release 2026c
sources.relevance: The de facto global registry of civil time zone identifiers, offsets and transition history; the release identifier is the versioning anchor for all zone-dependent computation.

sources.title: RFC 6557 — Procedures for Maintaining the Time Zone Database (BCP 175)
sources.relevance: Normative governance of the tz database: the TZ Coordinator role, proposal and decision process, release signing, and the explicit statement that the database records rather than sets civil time policy.

sources.title: Theory and pragmatics of the tz code and data
sources.relevance: First-party specification of Zone/Rule/Link semantics, naming and stability guarantees, zone1970.tab and zonenow.tab, and the explicit accuracy caveats for pre-1970 and future timestamps.

sources.title: RFC 9636 — The Time Zone Information Format (TZif)
sources.relevance: Normative binary projection of zone data: transition times, local time type records (utoff, isdst, desigidx), leap-second records, POSIX TZ footer and version 4 leap-table expiration.

sources.title: RFC 3339 — Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps
sources.relevance: The mandated timestamp profile for this model: full-date/full-time grammar, explicit offset or Z, the -00:00 unknown-offset convention, and 23:59:60 leap-second representation.

sources.title: RFC 9557 — Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps with Additional Information (IXDTF)
sources.relevance: Defines carrying time zone and calendar annotations alongside an instant, the critical-flag processing requirement, and the reinterpretation of Z as 'offset to local time unknown'.

sources.title: RFC 5545 — Internet Calendaring and Scheduling Core Object Specification (iCalendar)
sources.relevance: Normative semantics for VTIMEZONE observances, the RECUR value type, EXDATE/RDATE, DURATION and PERIOD, and the floating / UTC / TZID-bound date-time distinction.

sources.title: RFC 7529 — Non-Gregorian Recurrence Rules in the Internet Calendaring and Scheduling Core Object Specification (iCalendar)
sources.relevance: Binds recurrence expansion to a named calendar system via RSCALE using the Unicode calendar registry, and defines SKIP=OMIT/BACKWARD/FORWARD and leap-month 'L' notation.

sources.title: RFC 8984 — JSCalendar: A JSON Representation of Calendar Data
sources.relevance: An independent, non-iCalendar projection of the same temporal semantics: LocalDateTime vs UTCDateTime, timeZone, embedded timeZones, recurrenceRules and recurrenceOverrides, showWithoutTime.

sources.title: RFC 7808 — Time Zone Data Distribution Service (TZDIST)
sources.relevance: Normative model for versioning and distributing zone data: monolithic vs incremental versions, truncation with TZUNTIL, alias/canonical handling, expand and leapseconds actions, ETag and sync-token change detection.

sources.title: Unicode Technical Standard #35: Unicode Locale Data Markup Language (LDML), Part 4: Dates
sources.relevance: Normative calendar and era data structures (era code, start/end in proleptic Gregorian, inheritEras) and the stable CLDR timezone identifier layer with metazones and alias equivalences over the volatile tzdb.

sources.title: Unicode Technical Standard #35: LDML, Part 6: Supplemental
sources.relevance: Supplemental territory-scoped data: week data (first day of week, weekend days, minimum days), calendar preference by region, timezoneData, metazoneInfo, primaryZones and windowsZones.

sources.title: CLDR BCP 47 calendar key registry (common/bcp47/calendar.xml)
sources.relevance: The governed registry of calendar identifiers (u-ca values) referenced normatively by RFC 7529 and RFC 9557, including Hijri variants that differ by determination method and the deprecated islamicc alias.

sources.title: Resolution 4 of the 27th CGPM (2022): On the use and future development of UTC
sources.organization: Bureau International des Poids et Mesures (BIPM) / CGPM
sources.relevance: The decision that the maximum value of UT1-UTC will be increased in or before 2035, with CIPM to propose the new maximum and implementation plan; the governing lifecycle event for leap-second policy.

sources.title: IERS Bulletin C 72
sources.organization: International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service (IERS), Earth Orientation Centre
sources.relevance: The authoritative serial announcement of leap-second insertion or non-insertion; confirms no leap second at end of December 2026 and UTC-TAI = -37 s since 2017-01-01.

sources.title: leap-seconds.list
sources.relevance: Machine-readable leap-second table with NTP-epoch timestamps, cumulative TAI-UTC values, an explicit last-update line and an expiration line — the canonical model for temporal reference data that expires.

sources.title: Time Ontology in OWL
sources.version_or_date: W3C Candidate Recommendation Draft, 2022-11-15; namespace http://www.w3.org/2006/time#
sources.relevance: Format-neutral conceptual vocabulary for temporal entities: Instant, ProperInterval, Duration, GeneralDateTimeDescription, TemporalPosition with hasTRS, and the thirteen/fifteen Allen interval relations.

sources.title: Directive 2000/84/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 January 2001 on summer-time arrangements
sources.relevance: A concrete legal instrument that defines a daylight-saving rule (last Sunday in March to last Sunday in October, 01:00 GMT) and requires the Commission to publish a five-year timetable — the authority layer beneath tzdb entries.

sources.title: UK bank holidays (machine-readable calendar)
sources.relevance: A first-party public-authority holiday feed showing the minimum viable holiday record: division scoping, title, date, substitute-day notes, and a rolling publication horizon.

sources.title: 49 CFR Part 71 — Standard Time Zone Boundaries
sources.organization: U.S. Department of Transportation / Office of the Federal Register (govinfo)
sources.version_or_date: CFR annual edition, title 49 volume 1 (2024/2025 print)
sources.relevance: Demonstrates that civil zone boundaries are legally defined by an administering authority under the Uniform Time Act with a petition-and-rulemaking change process, described by county and municipal lines rather than by tz identifiers.

sources.title: FpML BusinessDayConventionEnum (fpml-enum-5-5)
sources.relevance: Normative enumeration and definitions of date-adjustment conventions (FOLLOWING, MODFOLLOWING, PRECEDING, MODPRECEDING, NEAREST, FRN, NONE, NotApplicable) used by working-day calendars.

sources.title: CLDR Releases / Downloads
sources.relevance: Authoritative release identity and date for the CLDR data version that must be pinned alongside a tzdb release when reproducing a temporal computation.

sources.title: BIPM Circular T archive (latest issue cirt.463)
sources.organization: Bureau International des Poids et Mesures (BIPM), Time Department
sources.relevance: Monthly authoritative publication relating UTC to its local realisations UTC(k); evidence that UTC is a computed, published scale with a serial, dated artifact rather than a static constant.

sources.title: Date and Time Formats (W3C Note, profile of ISO 8601)
sources.relevance: An accessible, citable statement of the ISO 8601 granularity ladder (year, year-month, date, date+hh:mm, +ss, +fraction) and the requirement that an adopting standard declare which granularities and offset forms it supports.

sources.title: Theory and pragmatics of the tz code and data
sources.relevance: Defines timezone naming policy, link and backward compatibility, zone table scope, and the limits of pre-1970 historical data.

sources.title: Leap second and UT1-UTC information
sources.organization: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.relevance: Inserted leap-second dates with MJD, the current TAI-UTC value of 37 seconds, and UT1-UTC and DUT1 series.

sources.title: THE LEAP SECOND
sources.organization: IERS Earth Orientation Center, Paris Observatory
sources.version_or_date: current IERS Earth Orientation Center page; last leap second 2017-01-01T00:00:00Z
sources.relevance: Authority and Bulletin C process for announcing leap seconds, and the requirement to keep UTC within 0.9 second of UT1.

sources.title: Unicode Locale Data Markup Language (LDML) Part 4: Dates
sources.version_or_date: UTS #35 living LDML (CLDR calendar types current on access date)
sources.relevance: BCP 47 calendar type inventory, era, month and week data, and locale display names for calendars and timezones.

sources.title: RFC 7529: Non-Gregorian Recurrence Rules in iCalendar
sources.relevance: RSCALE extension enabling recurrence evaluated on non-Gregorian calendars, and the record that CALSCALE was never used in practice.

sources.title: C132 - Holidays with Pay Convention (Revised), 1970 (No. 132)
sources.relevance: Distinguishes public and customary holidays from annual paid leave; the only retrieved primary instrument bearing on holiday semantics.

sources.title: How to Read the tz Database Source Files
sources.relevance: Field-level semantics of Zone and Rule lines: STDOFF, RULES, FORMAT, UNTIL, SAVE, LETTER and the AT clock suffixes.

bundles.name: Time base
bundles.description: The physical and computational substrate for locating an instant: named time scales, their epochs and mutual offsets, the governance of leap adjustments, and the rules for representing an instant with declared precision.
bundles.rationale: Every downstream temporal statement resolves, directly or indirectly, to an instant on a named scale. Scale choice and leap handling are authority-managed and change by international decision, so they must be modelled before zones, calendars or schedules.

layers.name: Time scale and epoch
layers.description: Named reference scales (UTC, TAI, UT1, GPS time, POSIX/Unix time, terrestrial time), their epochs, their continuity properties and the offsets that relate them.

findings.name: Time scale definition and inter-scale offset
findings.description: A time scale is a governed system for locating instants, characterised by its defining authority, epoch, unit, and whether it is continuous (TAI, GPS) or subject to discontinuities (UTC). Statements are only comparable when the scale is declared; the current relation UTC = TAI - 37 s has been in force since 2017-01-01 and is itself a dated fact.

questions.text: Which named time scale does this temporal value use, and is that scale explicitly declared or merely assumed?
answer_data: default scale for the containing model

questions.text: Which body defines and publishes this scale, and through which serial publication is its realisation disseminated?
Is the scale continuous, or may it contain inserted or removed seconds that break naive arithmetic?
What is the offset from this scale to UTC at a given instant, and from when is that offset valid?
Which scale is used for the underlying storage representation, and does it differ from the scale used for display or comparison?

data_elements.name: scaleId
data_elements.description: Stable identifier of the time scale (for example UTC, TAI, UT1, GPS, UNIX).

data_elements.name: epochInstant
data_elements.description: The instant from which the scale's count or numbering begins, expressed on a declared reference scale.

data_elements.name: continuityClass
data_elements.description: Whether the scale is continuous, stepped by leap adjustments, smeared, or unspecified.

data_elements.name: offsetToUtc
data_elements.description: Signed offset from this scale to UTC, valid over a stated period.

data_elements.name: definingAuthorityRef
data_elements.description: Reference to the organisation that defines the scale and to the serial publication that realises it.

artifacts.name: Time scale register
artifacts.description: The curated set of time scales recognised by the adopting Dimension, with epochs, continuity classes and inter-scale offset histories.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Governed scale identifiers (UTC, TAI, GPS, UT1) as authoritative master-system identifiers; the register itself carries a Dimension-assigned UUID and a release identifier.

artifacts.name: Scale realisation bulletin
artifacts.description: A dated, numbered publication relating the scale to its local realisations, such as BIPM Circular T.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Publisher's serial number plus issue date (for example Circular T 463 of 2026-08-11); never identified by date alone.

layers.name: Leap adjustment and UTC governance
layers.description: How leap seconds are decided, announced, tabulated, represented and retired, including the CGPM decision to raise the UT1-UTC tolerance by 2035.

findings.name: Leap adjustment decision, table and expiry
findings.description: Leap seconds are announced by IERS in serial Bulletin C notices, tabulated in a machine-readable list carrying an explicit expiration, represented in timestamps as second value 60, and are subject to a standing CGPM decision to increase the permitted UT1-UTC difference in or before 2035. A leap table is therefore a perishable artifact, not a constant.

questions.text: Which body decides a leap adjustment, and by which dated instrument was the most recent decision announced?
What is the cumulative TAI-UTC value at a given instant, and when does the consulted leap table expire?
How does this system represent or avoid the 60th second, and is that behaviour declared?
answer_data: leap representation policy (represent as :60, smear, reject, clamp)
smear window and shape if applicable

questions.text: What happens to stored durations and orderings computed before a leap adjustment took effect?
How will the planned change to the UT1-UTC tolerance by 2035 affect assumptions currently baked into this Dimension?
Is the leap table currently in use still valid, and what is done when it has expired?

data_elements.name: leapEventInstant
data_elements.description: The instant at which a leap adjustment takes or took effect, on the UTC scale.

data_elements.name: cumulativeTaiUtcOffset
data_elements.description: Cumulative TAI-UTC difference in whole seconds after the adjustment.

data_elements.name: leapTableExpiresAt
data_elements.description: The instant after which the leap-second table must not be relied upon.

data_elements.name: announcementRef
data_elements.description: Reference to the serial bulletin that announced the decision.

data_elements.name: leapHandlingPolicy
data_elements.description: Declared behaviour of this system when a leap second occurs or is encountered in input.

artifacts.name: Leap second table
artifacts.description: Machine-readable table of leap events with cumulative offsets, a last-update marker and an explicit expiration marker.
media_or_form: binary leap records inside a zone information file
artifacts.identity_strategy: Publisher URL plus the table's own last-update timestamp; supersession is by later last-update value, and the expiration value governs usability.

artifacts.name: Leap decision notice
artifacts.description: The numbered bulletin announcing insertion or non-insertion of a leap second at the next opportunity.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Issuing authority plus bulletin series and sequence number (for example IERS Bulletin C 72), with issue date recorded separately from effective date.

layers.name: Instant representation and precision
layers.description: How a single point in time is written down: the mandated timestamp profile, offset semantics, fractional precision, and the separation of event time from observation time.

findings.name: Instant representation profile
findings.description: An instant is recorded using an RFC 3339 date-time with an explicit numeric offset or Z, optionally annotated per RFC 9557 with the originating time zone and calendar. The distinct meanings of Z, +00:00 and -00:00, the declared fractional precision, and the separation of event time from observation or ingestion time are all part of the record's meaning.

questions.text: Does every recorded instant carry an explicit offset or Z, and are unqualified local times rejected at the boundary?
answer_data: validation error code for missing offset
count of legacy values lacking offset

questions.text: Is the offset a known local offset, an assertion of UTC preference, or a declaration that the local offset is unknown?
What fractional-second precision is stored, and is stored precision distinguished from measured precision?
Are event time and observation or ingestion time recorded separately for this record class?
When an instant is annotated with a time zone, is that annotation critical, and what must happen if it contradicts the offset?
answer_data: action on conflict (reject, prefer offset, prefer zone)

data_elements.name: instantValue
data_elements.description: The point in time, expressed with date, time and explicit offset or Z.

data_elements.name: zoneAnnotation
data_elements.description: Optional originating time zone identifier carried with the instant, with a criticality flag.

data_elements.name: calendarAnnotation
data_elements.description: Optional preferred calendar for presenting the instant, expressed as a registered calendar key.

data_elements.name: declaredPrecision
data_elements.description: The granularity actually asserted by the value, independent of the digits stored.

data_elements.name: observedAt
data_elements.description: When the value was observed, recorded or ingested, as distinct from when the described event occurred.

artifacts.name: Timestamp conformance profile
artifacts.description: A declared profile stating which granularities, offset forms, annotations and precision this Dimension accepts and emits, as required when adopting an ISO 8601 profile.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Dimension-assigned identifier plus semantic version; superseded profiles retained with effective-from and effective-until instants.

bundles.name: Civil time zone
bundles.description: The identity, offset history, resolution behaviour and legal basis of civil time zones — the machinery that converts between wall-clock time in a place and an instant.
bundles.rationale: Zone data is the single largest source of temporal defects: identifiers are aliased and unstable, rules change by decree with little notice, and local times can be ambiguous or non-existent. Each of these is a separately answerable body of context.

layers.name: Zone identity and registry
layers.description: How a time zone is named and identified, the canonical versus alias distinction, the stable CLDR identifier layer, and what must never be used as an identifier.

findings.name: Zone identifier, canonicality and aliases
findings.description: A civil zone is identified by a tz identifier in Area/Location form, which may be a primary zone or a backward-compatibility link to another zone. CLDR maintains a deliberately more stable identifier layer with documented alias equivalences, because zone names, boundaries, offsets and abbreviations are explicitly not all stable interfaces.

questions.text: Which identifier scheme is this zone identifier drawn from, and is the value canonical or an alias?
Which stable identifier does this Dimension persist when the upstream registry renames or relinks a zone?
answer_data: persisted identifier layer (tz canonical, CLDR BCP47 key, internal surrogate)

questions.text: Are zone abbreviations, numeric offsets or country codes ever used to identify a zone in this system?
What happens to stored references when a zone is split, merged or retired upstream?
Which geographic region does this identifier actually cover, and is that coverage authoritative for jurisdictional purposes?
answer_data: region description from the zone table

data_elements.name: tzId
data_elements.description: Time zone identifier in Area/Location form as published by the tz database.

data_elements.name: isCanonical
data_elements.description: Whether the identifier is a primary zone rather than a backward link.

data_elements.name: aliasOf
data_elements.description: The canonical zone identifier that this alias resolves to.

data_elements.name: stableZoneKey
data_elements.description: The stability-preserving identifier layer used for persistence, such as the CLDR BCP47 timezone key.

data_elements.name: coveredRegionRef
data_elements.description: Reference to the jurisdiction or region the zone represents, drawn from the place model.

data_elements.name: metazoneRef
data_elements.description: Grouping used for shared display names across a period, where a presentation layer needs it.

artifacts.name: Zone identifier crosswalk
artifacts.description: Mapping between tz canonical identifiers, backward links, CLDR stable keys, legacy platform identifiers and any internal surrogates.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Keyed on the tz canonical identifier as the authoritative master-system identifier; the crosswalk carries a Dimension UUID plus the tzdb and CLDR release identifiers it was built against.

layers.name: Offset rule and transition history
layers.description: The rule and transition structures that give a zone its offset at any instant, including daylight indicators, designations, projections and truncation.

findings.name: Offset transition and local time type
findings.description: A zone's behaviour is a sorted series of transitions, each selecting a local time type consisting of a UTC offset, a daylight indicator and a designation. Rules need not alternate between two states, may change more than twice per year, and future behaviour beyond the last explicit transition is governed by a projected rule string or by a stated validity limit.

questions.text: What is the complete ordered series of offset transitions for this zone over the period the data must serve?
answer_data: transition instants on the reference scale

questions.text: Until what instant is the zone data explicitly valid, and how is behaviour beyond that point derived?
Was a given transition a historical fact, a scheduled future change, or a prediction from a repeating rule?
Which upstream release supplied this transition series, and has any transition changed between releases?
Is the recorded pre-1970 history evidence-backed or reconstructed, and is that distinction visible to consumers?
Which projection formats must this transition series be emitted in, and are they lossless with respect to each other?

data_elements.name: transitionAt
data_elements.description: The instant at which a new local time type takes effect.

data_elements.name: offsetBefore
data_elements.description: UTC offset in force immediately before the transition.

data_elements.name: offsetAfter
data_elements.description: UTC offset in force immediately after the transition.

data_elements.name: isDaylight
data_elements.description: Whether the resulting local time type is a daylight saving observance.

data_elements.name: designation
data_elements.description: Abbreviation displayed for the local time type; explicitly not usable as an identifier.

data_elements.name: validUntil
data_elements.description: Upper bound of asserted validity for truncated zone data.

data_elements.name: futureRuleExpression
data_elements.description: Rule used to project transitions beyond the last explicit entry.

artifacts.name: Zone information file
artifacts.description: Binary projection of the transition series, local time types, designations, leap records and projection footer.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Zone canonical identifier plus the producing release identifier and format version; content hash recorded for integrity.

artifacts.name: Zone observance component
artifacts.description: Textual calendaring projection of a zone as standard and daylight observances with offsets, names and recurrence or explicit dates.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Zone identifier plus validity upper bound; alias origin recorded when the component was requested under a non-canonical name.

layers.name: Local time anomaly resolution
layers.description: Deterministic handling of wall-clock times that do not exist or occur twice, and of timestamps whose offset contradicts their declared zone.

findings.name: Gap, overlap and offset-conflict policy
findings.description: Around a transition, a local wall-clock time may be skipped or may occur twice, and a supplied offset may disagree with the supplied zone. A conforming system must declare a deterministic resolution policy; where a zone annotation is marked critical the inconsistency must be acted upon rather than silently ignored.

questions.text: When a stated local time falls in a transition gap, is it rejected, shifted forward, or shifted by the gap duration?
When a stated local time is ambiguous, is the earlier or later occurrence chosen, and can the caller override?
If the supplied offset contradicts the supplied zone identifier, which wins, and is the annotation critical?
Is the resolved offset persisted alongside the local time so the resolution is reproducible later?
How are recurring local-time series handled when a future instance lands in a gap created by a later rule change?

data_elements.name: gapPolicy
data_elements.description: Declared behaviour for non-existent local times.

data_elements.name: overlapPolicy
data_elements.description: Declared behaviour for ambiguous local times.

data_elements.name: resolvedOffset
data_elements.description: The offset actually selected when a local time was resolved to an instant.

data_elements.name: offsetZoneConflictAction
data_elements.description: Action taken when a supplied offset and zone disagree.

artifacts.name: Disambiguation policy statement
artifacts.description: Published statement of gap, overlap and conflict handling, so that consumers can reproduce a resolution.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Dimension-assigned identifier with semantic version and effective-from instant; changes are breaking and require a new version.

layers.name: Zone legal authority and change process
layers.description: The legal instruments and administrative processes by which jurisdictions set standard time and daylight saving arrangements, and the distinction between those instruments and their database mirror.

findings.name: Civil time decree and its mirroring
findings.description: Standard time and daylight saving arrangements are set by legal instruments — directives, statutes, regulations and proclamations — with a defined administering authority and change procedure. The tz database mirrors the resulting consensus on the ground and its coordinator explicitly does not set policy, so the legal instrument, not the database entry, is the authority of record.

questions.text: Which authority is legally competent to change standard time or daylight arrangements for this territory?
By which dated instrument was the current arrangement established, and where was it officially published?
What is the procedure and evidentiary threshold for changing a boundary or an exemption?
When does the change take legal effect, and how much notice was given before that instant?
Who owns the record of this arrangement in the adopting Dimension, and who mirrors it into machine data?
answer_data: upstream mirror release in which it appeared

questions.text: Is the machine data currently consistent with the legal instrument, and what is done while they diverge?

data_elements.name: instrumentIdentifier
data_elements.description: Authoritative identifier of the legal instrument, such as a CELEX number, statute citation or regulation part.

data_elements.name: competentAuthority
data_elements.description: The body empowered to make or amend the arrangement.

data_elements.name: effectiveAt
data_elements.description: Instant at which the arrangement takes legal effect.

data_elements.name: announcedAt
data_elements.description: Instant at which the change was publicly announced, recorded separately from the effective instant.

data_elements.name: territoryRef
data_elements.description: Jurisdiction or sub-jurisdictional division to which the arrangement applies.

data_elements.name: mirroredInRelease
data_elements.description: Upstream reference-data release in which the change first appeared.

artifacts.name: Legal instrument citation record
artifacts.description: Structured citation of the statute, directive, regulation or proclamation governing civil time for a territory, with official publication reference.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Official instrument identifier from the issuing legal system as the authoritative master identifier; a Dimension UUID only where none exists.

artifacts.name: Zone change notice
artifacts.description: Operational notice issued when a jurisdiction's zone or daylight rule changes, carrying announcement instant, effective instant and affected zone identifiers.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Sequential notice number within the Dimension, plus announcement instant and the upstream release identifier that carried the change.

bundles.name: Calendar system
bundles.description: How days are grouped into months, years, eras and weeks, and how those systems are identified, structured and defaulted by territory.
bundles.rationale: Calendar choice is not presentation: recurrence expansion, era-based year numbering and week arithmetic produce different dates in different calendars, and the calendar identifier is normatively required by recurrence and timestamp annotation standards.

layers.name: Calendar identity and structure
layers.description: Registered calendar identifiers, their classification, intercalation and leap-month structure, and their deprecation and alias handling.

findings.name: Calendar system identity, type and intercalation
findings.description: A calendar system is identified by a registered key from the Unicode calendar registry, which recurrence and timestamp standards reference normatively. The registry distinguishes systems that differ only in determination method — tabular civil, tabular astronomical, Umm al-Qura and sighting-based Hijri variants — and marks deprecated keys with preferred replacements; leap months are denoted by an L suffix in recurrence contexts.

questions.text: Which registered calendar key identifies this system, and is that key current or deprecated in favour of another?
Is the system solar, lunar or lunisolar, and does it use intercalary days, intercalary months or both?
Where two keys describe the same tradition but differ in determination method, which one governs this record?
How are leap months represented and ordered when a date or recurrence falls in one?
answer_data: position relative to the base month
behaviour when the leap month is absent in a target year

questions.text: Which calendar is assumed when none is declared, and is that assumption territory-dependent?
Can this calendar's dates be converted losslessly to and from the proleptic Gregorian representation used for storage?

data_elements.name: calendarKey
data_elements.description: Registered calendar identifier used in annotations and recurrence scales.

data_elements.name: astronomicalClass
data_elements.description: Whether the calendar is solar, lunar or lunisolar.

data_elements.name: determinationMethod
data_elements.description: Whether dates are fixed by tabular rule, astronomical computation or observation.

data_elements.name: intercalationRule
data_elements.description: Rule governing leap days or leap months.

data_elements.name: deprecatedAlias
data_elements.description: Superseded key that resolves to this calendar.

artifacts.name: Calendar registry entry
artifacts.description: The adopted subset of the calendar registry, recording key, description, since-version and deprecation state for each calendar supported by the Dimension.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Registry key as the governed global identifier, qualified by the registry release version the extract was taken from.

layers.name: Era and year numbering
layers.description: Eras within a calendar, their boundaries expressed in proleptic Gregorian terms, their ordering and inheritance, and the events that add or redefine them.

findings.name: Era boundaries, ordering and change events
findings.description: An era is a named span within a calendar system with a mnemonic code, a numeric type for name lookup, and start and end dates expressed as proleptic Gregorian dates; eras are ordered by start date and may be inherited between related calendars. Eras are mutable reference data: a new era can be proclaimed and existing systems must absorb it.

questions.text: Which era does a given date fall in, and how is the era boundary expressed unambiguously?
What identifies the era stably — the mnemonic code or the numeric type used for name lookup?
Does this calendar inherit eras from another calendar, and does that inheritance affect ordering?
What process adds a new era, and what is the lead time between proclamation and effect?
answer_data: data release in which the era appeared

questions.text: Are year numbers within the era counted forward only, and how are dates before the calendar's epoch expressed?

data_elements.name: eraCode
data_elements.description: Mnemonic identifier for the era within its calendar system.

data_elements.name: eraStartDate
data_elements.description: Era start expressed as a proleptic Gregorian date.

data_elements.name: eraEndDate
data_elements.description: Era end expressed as a proleptic Gregorian date, absent for the current era.

data_elements.name: calendarRef
data_elements.description: The calendar system the era belongs to.

data_elements.name: yearInEra
data_elements.description: Year number counted within the era.

artifacts.name: Era table
artifacts.description: Ordered table of eras per calendar system with codes, numeric types, boundaries and inheritance.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Calendar key plus era code as compound authoritative identifier; the table carries the data release version it was derived from.

layers.name: Week rules and territory defaults
layers.description: Territory-scoped week data and calendar preference: first day of week, minimum days in the first week, weekend days, and the ISO week-date system.

findings.name: Week rule set and weekend definition
findings.description: First day of week, minimum days in the first week and weekend start and end are territory-scoped supplemental data, and can be overridden by an explicit region key. Week numbering under the ISO rules is itself a distinct registered calendar key, and recurrence rules carry their own week-start parameter that must not be silently inherited from locale.

questions.text: Which territory's week data governs this computation, and how was that territory determined?
What are the first day of week, the minimum days in the first week and the weekend days for that territory?
Does week numbering follow the ISO week-date rules or the territory's own rules, and is that choice declared?
Is the week-start used in recurrence expansion the same as the locale week-start, and what happens if they differ?
How is a weekend that is not Saturday and Sunday represented in working-day calculations?

data_elements.name: firstDayOfWeek
data_elements.description: Territory-scoped first day of the week.

data_elements.name: minDaysInFirstWeek
data_elements.description: Minimum days that must fall in the first week of a year for it to count as week one.

data_elements.name: weekendDays
data_elements.description: Set of days treated as the weekend in the territory.

data_elements.name: weekNumberingSystem
data_elements.description: Which week-numbering rules apply, including the ISO week-date calendar key.

data_elements.name: recurrenceWeekStart
data_elements.description: Week-start parameter used by a recurrence rule, independent of locale data.

artifacts.name: Week data profile
artifacts.description: Adopted territory-by-territory week and weekend data with declared overrides, used as the base of all working-day computation.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Territory code as key, qualified by the locale data release version; overrides carry an explicit owner and effective-from instant.

bundles.name: Temporal value shapes
bundles.description: The reusable, embeddable value objects this mix-in offers to every other model: instants, intervals, durations, granularity, indeterminacy and the binding contract that says how a temporal field is to be interpreted.
bundles.rationale: As a mix-in, the model's principal deliverable is a small set of precisely specified value shapes plus an explicit declaration of how each temporal field is bound. Without that declaration, floating, zoned and absolute times are indistinguishable in storage and silently produce wrong results.

layers.name: Instant, interval and duration
layers.description: The core value shapes and their arithmetic: zero-extent instants, proper intervals, exact versus nominal durations, and period forms.

findings.name: Core temporal value shapes and duration arithmetic
findings.description: Temporal entities divide into instants of zero extent and intervals with extent, with proper intervals having distinct beginning and end. Periods are expressed either as start and end or as start and duration, and durations split into exact machine quantities and nominal calendar-clock descriptions whose length depends on where they are applied — a distinction that matters at transitions and at month boundaries.

questions.text: Is this value an instant or an interval, and if an interval, are its endpoints distinct?
Is the interval expressed as start and end or as start and duration, and are the endpoints inclusive or exclusive?
Is the duration an exact quantity or a nominal calendar description, and which units may it carry?
How is a nominal duration added across a zone transition or a short or long month?
Can an interval be unbounded at either end, and how is that represented distinctly from a missing value?

data_elements.name: start
data_elements.description: Beginning of the interval, or the instant itself for a zero-extent value.

data_elements.name: end
data_elements.description: End of the interval when expressed explicitly.

data_elements.name: duration
data_elements.description: Length of the interval expressed as a duration when the end is not stated explicitly.

data_elements.name: durationKind
data_elements.description: Whether the duration is an exact quantity or a nominal calendar-clock description.

data_elements.name: endpointInclusivity
data_elements.description: Declared inclusivity of the interval endpoints.

findings.inline_only_rationale: These are embedded value objects with no independent existence, custody or lifecycle: an interval or duration is always a property of some host record in a sibling model and is created, versioned and deleted with that host. Materialising them as standalone artifacts would create identifiers that no authority maintains and would invite reference drift; the model therefore ships them as inline shapes plus the binding declaration artifact in the sibling layer.

layers.name: Granularity and indeterminacy
layers.description: Declared precision, date-only versus date-time values, open-ended and partially known temporal statements, and how uncertainty is surfaced rather than fabricated.

findings.name: Declared granularity, all-day values and open endpoints
findings.description: A temporal statement carries a granularity that must be declared rather than inferred from the digits present, ranging from year through fractional second. Date-only values and all-day semantics are distinct from midnight-precision date-times, and an adopting profile must state which granularities and offset forms it supports.

questions.text: What granularity does this value actually assert, and is that recorded separately from its serialised form?
Is this a date-only or all-day value, and is it therefore zone-independent?
Which granularities and offset forms does this Dimension's adopted profile accept on input and emit on output?
How is a value that is known only approximately, or only to a bounded range, represented without inventing precision?
answer_data: representation chosen (bounded interval, granularity downgrade, qualifier)

questions.text: Is comparison between values of different granularity defined, and what does it return when they overlap?

data_elements.name: granularity
data_elements.description: Asserted precision of the value, from year to fractional second.

data_elements.name: isAllDay
data_elements.description: Whether the value denotes a whole day rather than a point within it.

data_elements.name: boundedRange
data_elements.description: Interval within which the true value is asserted to lie, used instead of false precision.

data_elements.name: openEndpoint
data_elements.description: Marks a start or end as open or unbounded rather than unknown.

artifacts.name: Temporal precision profile
artifacts.description: The Dimension's declaration of accepted and emitted granularities, all-day semantics, and representation of bounded or open values.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Dimension-assigned identifier and semantic version; effective-from and effective-until instants recorded on each version.

layers.name: Temporal binding contract
layers.description: The per-field declaration of whether a temporal value is floating, zoned or absolute, and which companion fields must accompany it.

findings.name: Floating, zoned and absolute binding
findings.description: Three bindings exist and must be distinguished per field: a floating local value that occurs at the same wall-clock reading everywhere, a local value bound to a named zone, and an absolute instant with an explicit offset or Z. The binding determines which companion fields are mandatory and which operations are valid, and it is a semantic property of the field, not of its serialisation.

questions.text: Which binding does this field use, and where is that binding declared for machine consumption?
Which companion fields are mandatory for this binding — zone identifier, calendar key, granularity, resolved offset?
Is a floating value ever silently converted to an absolute instant on storage or transport?
When the value crosses a system boundary, which annotations travel with it and which are critical?
Which binding should be chosen for a newly modelled field, and on what test?
answer_data: decision test (does the moment shift with the observer)

data_elements.name: bindingMode
data_elements.description: Declared binding: floating, zoned or absolute.

data_elements.name: zoneRef
data_elements.description: Zone identifier required when the binding is zoned.

data_elements.name: calendarRef
data_elements.description: Calendar key required when the field's meaning depends on a non-default calendar.

data_elements.name: annotationCriticality
data_elements.description: Whether accompanying annotations must be honoured or may be ignored by a receiver.

artifacts.name: Field binding declaration
artifacts.description: Machine-readable register of every temporal field exposed by the adopting Dimension with its binding, companion field requirements and validation rules.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Fully qualified field path within the owning model as the master identifier; register version tracks additions and binding changes, which are breaking.

bundles.name: Recurrence and scheduling rules
bundles.description: Rules that generate sets of dates or instants, their exceptions and overrides, and their behaviour under non-Gregorian calendar scales.
bundles.rationale: Recurrence is where calendar, zone and week data combine and where most silent divergence between implementations appears. Its semantics are normatively specified and must be modelled separately from the values it generates.

layers.name: Recurrence rule semantics
layers.description: The structure and evaluation of a recurrence rule: frequency, interval, by-part filters, week start, and the bounds that terminate the set.

findings.name: Recurrence rule structure and expansion
findings.description: A recurrence rule has a required frequency and optional interval, by-part filters, week start and a terminating count or until value, with count and until mutually exclusive. Expansion is anchored on the series start value, and by-position selection applies after the other filters, so an unanchored or unbounded rule is not evaluable without an explicit expansion window.

questions.text: What frequency, interval and by-part filters define this rule, and in what order are they applied?
What anchors the expansion, and does the anchor itself belong to the generated set?
Is the rule bounded by a count or by an until value, and does the until value match the anchor's value type and binding?
For an unbounded rule, what expansion window is used and who sets it?
Which week start applies, and how does changing it alter the generated set?
When the underlying zone rules change, are previously expanded instances recomputed or frozen?

data_elements.name: frequency
data_elements.description: Required base frequency of the recurrence.

data_elements.name: interval
data_elements.description: How many frequency units separate occurrences.

data_elements.name: byParts
data_elements.description: Filter components such as by-day, by-month-day, by-month and by-position.

data_elements.name: until
data_elements.description: Inclusive upper bound of the recurrence set.

data_elements.name: count
data_elements.description: Number of occurrences generated, mutually exclusive with the until bound.

data_elements.name: anchorValue
data_elements.description: The series start from which expansion proceeds.

artifacts.name: Recurrence rule expression
artifacts.description: The stored, portable expression of the rule together with its anchor, binding mode and expansion window.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by the owning series identifier plus rule sequence position; a Dimension UUID is assigned where the rule is reused standalone.

artifacts.name: Expanded occurrence set
artifacts.description: Materialised occurrences for a stated window, recording the zone and calendar data releases used so the expansion is reproducible.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Series identifier plus window bounds plus the reference-data release identifiers used; regenerated sets are new artifacts, not edits.

layers.name: Recurrence exceptions and calendar scale
layers.description: Excluded and added dates, per-occurrence overrides and their identity, and expansion under a non-Gregorian calendar scale with skip behaviour.

findings.name: Exceptions, overrides and non-Gregorian expansion
findings.description: A recurrence set is modified by excluded dates, additional dates and per-occurrence overrides keyed by the occurrence's original value; an override key that matches no generated occurrence yields an extra occurrence rather than an error. When expansion runs on a non-Gregorian scale, an explicit scale parameter selects the calendar and a skip parameter determines the treatment of dates that do not exist in the target year.

questions.text: How is a single occurrence identified so that an override or cancellation can target it unambiguously?
answer_data: behaviour when the key matches no occurrence

questions.text: Which dates are excluded and which are added outside the rule, and who authorised each?
Which calendar scale governs expansion, and is it declared explicitly rather than inherited?
What happens when a generated date does not exist in the target year — omit, move backward or move forward?
answer_data: worked example for a leap-day rule

questions.text: Do all consuming implementations expand this rule to the same set, and how was that verified?
Are overrides preserved when the base rule is edited, and how are orphaned overrides detected?

data_elements.name: excludedDates
data_elements.description: Dates removed from the generated set.

data_elements.name: addedDates
data_elements.description: Dates added to the set outside the rule.

data_elements.name: occurrenceOverrides
data_elements.description: Map from an occurrence key to a patch of that occurrence's properties, including cancellation.

data_elements.name: recurrenceScale
data_elements.description: Registered calendar key governing expansion.

data_elements.name: skipBehaviour
data_elements.description: Treatment of generated dates that do not exist in the target year or month.

data_elements.name: leapMonthMarker
data_elements.description: Notation identifying a leap month in by-month filters.

artifacts.name: Recurrence override set
artifacts.description: The stored collection of exclusions, additions and per-occurrence patches for a series, with authorisation metadata.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Series identifier plus occurrence key; each override records the actor and the instant at which it was applied.

bundles.name: Observance and working day
bundles.description: Days that carry civil or cultural weight: proclaimed public holidays, religious and cultural observances, and the working-day calendars and date-adjustment conventions built from them.
bundles.rationale: Holiday and observance data has a different authority model from zone data — it is proclaimed per jurisdiction, published on a rolling horizon and frequently amended — and it feeds date arithmetic that has direct legal and financial consequence.

layers.name: Public holiday proclamation
layers.description: Holidays declared by a competent authority for a jurisdiction or division, their day-off status, substitute days and publication horizon.

findings.name: Proclaimed holiday instance and substitution
findings.description: A public holiday is a dated instance scoped to a jurisdictional division, carrying a title, the date actually observed, and notes recording substitution where the nominal date falls on a non-working day. Authoritative feeds publish a bounded forward horizon and include one-off holidays, so a holiday set is a per-jurisdiction, per-year assertion rather than a permanent rule.

questions.text: Which jurisdiction or sub-jurisdictional division does this holiday apply to, and do divisions within the same state differ?
answer_data: list of divisions where the holiday does not apply

questions.text: Which authority proclaimed the holiday, and under what instrument?
Is the observed date the nominal date or a substitute, and what rule produced the substitution?
Does the holiday confer a non-working day, and for whom — all employers, public sector only, or specific sectors?
How far forward is the holiday calendar authoritatively published, and what is done beyond that horizon?
